label: VMware vSphere

corePack.why: Datastore fill is the most common preventable VM outage.
corePack.whyNow: Guests freeze when the datastore is full, often with no guest-level clue.
corePack.metric: Datastore capacity used percent and days-to-full

corePack.why: CPU ready time is the hypervisor telling you VMs are queued, not busy.
corePack.whyNow: Guest CPU looks fine while applications wait on pCPU.

corePack.why: Snapshot sprawl burns datastore space and slows storage.
corePack.whyNow: Forgotten backup snapshots are a silent capacity leak.
corePack.metric: Snapshot count and age per VM

corePack.why: vCenter health is the control plane for every other vSphere signal.
corePack.whyNow: If vCenter is sick you cannot manage HA, DRS, or alarms.

corePack.why: HA failover means a host died and VMs restarted elsewhere.
corePack.whyNow: You need remaining-host capacity and hardware root cause immediately.

corePack.why: Datastore latency is the storage path before capacity is exhausted.
corePack.whyNow: Latency pages earlier than fill for I/O-bound estates.

corePack.why: Aged snapshots are the actionable follow-up to snapshot sprawl.
corePack.whyNow: Age, not count, tells you which disks to consolidate first.

valueHypothesis: vSphere monitoring should start with datastore space, CPU ready, snapshots, vCenter health, and HA failovers—the signals VMware operators use to keep guests running—not every HCI neighbour that mentions a VM.
rationale: vSphere operations literature and Splunk Lantern virtualization content consistently lead with datastore capacity, CPU ready, snapshot hygiene, vCenter health, and HA events.
